# An Apology for Idlers

"BOSWELL: We grow weary when idle."

"JOHNSON: That is, sir, because others being busy, we want company; but if we were idle, there would be no growing weary; we should all entertain one another."

At present, everyone is expected to take up some lucrative profession and pursue it with something close to enthusiasm, on pain of being convicted in absentia of _lèse_-respectability. In such a climate, a word from the other side, from those who are content once they have enough and who like to look on and enjoy themselves in the meantime, may sound like bravado and boasting. It should not. Idleness, so called, does not mean doing nothing. It means doing a great deal that the ruling class does not recognise in its dogmatic formularies, and it has as much right to state its case as industry does. Admittedly, people who refuse to enter the great handicap race for sixpenny pieces are both an insult and a disappointment to those who run it. A fine fellow, of whom we see many, makes up his mind, votes for the sixpences and, in the emphatic American phrase, "goes for" them. As he ploughs wearily up the road, his resentment is easy to understand when he notices cool persons in the meadows beside it, lying with a handkerchief over their ears and a glass at their elbow. Diogenes's indifference touched Alexander in a very tender spot. Where was the glory of taking Rome for those tumultuous barbarians who poured into the Senate house and found the Fathers sitting silent, unmoved by their success? It is galling to toil upward, scale the steep hilltops, and then find humanity indifferent to the achievement. So physicists condemn the unphysical, financiers barely tolerate those who know little of stocks, literary people despise the unlettered, and people of every pursuit unite in disparaging those who have none.

That is one difficulty of the subject, but not the greatest. Nobody can imprison you for speaking against industry, though you can be sent to Coventry for speaking like a fool. With most subjects, the hardest thing is to treat them well, so please remember that this is an apology. A great deal can certainly be argued sensibly in favour of diligence. There is, however, something to be said against it, and that is what I mean to say here. Stating one argument does not mean being deaf to all the others. A man who has written a book of travels in Montenegro has not thereby sworn never to visit Richmond.

Surely people ought to be a good deal idle in youth. Here and there a Lord Macaulay may come away from school honours with his wits intact, but most boys pay so dearly for their medals that they never afterwards have a shot in their locker, and they begin the world bankrupt. The same holds for the whole period in which a young man is educating himself or letting others educate him. It must have been a very foolish old gentleman who said to Johnson at Oxford: "Young man, ply your book diligently now, and acquire a stock of knowledge; for when years come upon you, you will find that poring upon books will be but an irksome task." He seems not to have realised that many things besides reading grow irksome, and not a few become impossible, by the time a man needs spectacles and cannot walk without a stick. Books are good in their way, but they are a mighty bloodless substitute for life. It seems a pity to sit, like the Lady of Shalott, gazing into a mirror with your back to all the bustle and glamour of reality. And, as the old anecdote reminds us, a man who reads very hard will have little time left for thought.

If you look back on your own education, I am sure you will not regret the full, vivid, instructive hours of truancy. What you would rather cancel are the dull stretches spent half asleep in class. I have attended a good many lectures myself. I still remember that the spinning of a top is a case of Kinetic Stability, and that Emphyteusis is not a disease, nor Stillicide a crime. I would not willingly give up such scraps of learning, yet I value them less than certain other odds and ends I picked up in the open street while playing truant. This is not the place to enlarge on that great school, the favourite of Dickens and of Balzac, which turns out many inglorious masters in the Science of the Aspects of Life every year. It is enough to say that a lad who learns nothing in the streets has no faculty for learning at all. Nor is the truant confined to the streets. If he likes, he can walk out through the garden suburbs into the country, settle by some tuft of lilacs over a burn, and smoke countless pipes to the sound of water on the stones. A bird will sing in the thicket. There he may fall into a vein of kindly thought and see things from a new perspective. If this is not education, what is? We can imagine Mr. Worldly Wiseman coming upon such a young man, and the conversation that would follow:

"How now, young fellow, what dost thou here?"

"Truly, sir, I take mine ease."
